text:
The Defense Health Agency (DHA) and Walter Reed National Military Medical Center’s 3D Medical Applications Center (3D MAC) have received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) premarket clearance for the 3D MAC Titanium Cranial Plate (TCP) System.

It marks the first FDA-cleared implant granted to a point-of-care institution, claimed 3D Systems, and the patient-specific implant will be used to treat U.S. active duty personnel and service members suffering from traumatic head injuries.

3D Systems worked with 3D MAC on the device over a multi-year collaboration aimed at advancing additive manufacturing in clinical settings. The 3D Medical Applications Center, based at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, produces patient-specific anatomical models, surgical guides and implants for service members and veterans. The clearance marked 3D MAC’s first FDA-cleared medical device.

Building a regulatory pathway

3D Systems said it provided expertise in process controls, device design optimization, additive manufacturing workflows and regulatory strategy to support 3D MAC through the clearance process, covering design, validation and regulatory submission. The company also worked with 3D MAC to establish a quality management system for the program.

“We believe point-of-care manufacturing is transforming the future of healthcare by bringing personalized medical devices closer to the patient,” said Jeff Graves, President and Chief Executive Officer at 3D Systems.

“Our unique collaborations with the U.S. Defense Health Agency and the Department of Veterans Affairs underscore our leadership in this space and reinforce our commitment to expanding this business as a long-term growth driver for 3D Systems.”

Company points to broader point-of-care push

3D Systems said the clearance strengthens its relationships with the DHA and the Department of Veterans Affairs and positions the company to support further point-of-care medical manufacturing initiatives.

“This clearance underscores the power of combining clinical innovation with deep expertise in additive manufacturing and regulatory compliance,” said Natalie Byrnes, Manager of Product Development, Patient Specific Medical Technology at 3D Systems.

“We are honored to help enable expanded access to personalized care delivered at the point of treatment.”

text:
New York — Indian American Army surgeon Maj. Jagatkumar Patel has helped develop a minimally invasive technique to remove certain brain tumors through the nose, allowing patients to avoid open-skull surgery and recover more quickly.

Patel and Army neurosurgeon Lt. Col. Charles Miller developed the approach for tumors located at the base of the skull, according to the Pentagon.

“Historically, most of these surgeries were done open, which is a much more challenging procedure for the patient,” Patel said.

“Today, if a tumor is the appropriate size and location, open surgery just isn’t necessary,” he added. “Through the nose, we get the best access and the best chance of complete removal.”

Patel and Miller recently used the procedure to treat Marine Staff Sgt. Andy Archer, who had experienced severe headaches for 15 years.

After Archer began developing vision problems, an MRI revealed a tumor measuring 4.4 centimeters, roughly the size of a golf ball. The tumor was located in front of the pituitary gland and was pressing against his optic nerve.

Archer was referred to Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland, where Patel and Miller decided to remove the tumor entirely through the nasal passages.

Patel developed the surgical route through Archer’s complex nasal anatomy and used an endoscopic camera to provide a high-definition, close-up view of the tumor on a monitor. Miller then dissected and removed the growth.

“If he needs to get to critical structures, I can drive the camera closer, so he has perfect visualization,” Patel said.

He described the operation as a collaborative effort, crediting Miller with safely removing the tumor once access had been established.

“My skills in navigating the nasal approach are only useful because he is skilled enough to completely remove the tumor once we get there,” Patel said. “It is a true team effort.”

Two days after the procedure, Archer was sitting up in the surgical intensive care unit with no visible signs of major brain surgery. His vision had also begun to improve.

Patel said the minimally invasive approach can be more technically demanding and is suitable only when a tumor is located in an area that can be safely reached through the nose.

“I don’t think anyone else in the Defense Health Agency has this kind of team performing these complex skull base surgeries,” he said. (Source: IANS)

text:
Spark Biomedical, a commercial-stage bioelectronic medicine company announced its participation in the 2026 Military Health System Research Symposium (MHSRS), taking place August 3–6 at the Gaylord Palms Resort and Convention Center in Kissimmee, Florida. The company will present two scientific posters exploring applications of its transcutaneous auricular neurostimulation (tAN®) platform for cognitive performance and sleep in operational and military health contexts.

Michael Darrow, PhD, Spark’s Director of Research Innovations, will present “Enhancing Warfighter Readiness with Wearable Auricular Neurostimulation: Development and Clinical Evaluation.” The poster examines how Spark’s military grade device, HAWK, powered by tAN®, reduces perceived stress and associated physiological biomarkers.

Navid Khodaparast, PhD, Spark’s Chief Science Officer will present “Anxiety and Sleep in first responders: Wearable Auricular Neurostimulation to Improve Stress Resilience and Sleep in First Responders: Decentralized Clinical Trial Results” The poster will demonstrate how daily tAN® sessions in first responders can significantly reduce anxiety, improve sleep quality, and overall wellbeing.

MHSRS is the Department of Defense’s premier scientific conference dedicated to military medical research, bringing together military, federal, and civilian researchers to advance the health and readiness of service members. Spark’s presence at MHSRS reflects a strategic expansion of its tAN® platform beyond clinical and consumer settings into the military-ready space, extending the company’s research base to the operational demands of service members and first responders.

“Readiness starts with resilience,” said Navid Khodaparast, PhD, Chief Science Officer of Spark Biomedical. “Our research demonstrates how non-invasive auricular neurostimulation may help reduce stress, improve sleep, and support the health and performance of service members and first responders.”

The Defense Health Agency has awarded 12 companies positions on a combined $300 million indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract to support deployment activities for the Program Executive Office, Defense Healthcare Management Systems, or PEO DHMS.

Each awardee is guaranteed a minimum of $10,000, with the contract’s combined ceiling set at $300 million. The ordering period spans a one-year base period along with four one-year options and is scheduled to run from August 2026 through August 2031.

Defense Health Agency Media Advisory

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE July 27, 2026

TRICARE authorizes temporary prescription refill waiver for Wasco County, Oregon, due to the Grasshopper Fire

FALLS CHURCH, Virginia – The Defense Health Agency announced that TRICARE beneficiaries for Wasco County, Oregon, may receive emergency prescription refills now through Aug. 6, due to the Grasshopper Fire.

To receive an emergency refill of prescription medications, TRICARE beneficiaries should take their prescription bottle to any TRICARE retail network pharmacy. If the bottle is unavailable or the label is damaged or missing, beneficiaries should contact Express Scripts, Inc., or their retail network pharmacy for assistance.

To find a network pharmacy, beneficiaries may call Express Scripts at 1-877-363-1303, or search the https://militaryrx.express-scripts.com/find-pharmacy.

If possible, visit the pharmacy where the prescription was filled. Prescriptions filled by a retail chain may be filled at another store in that chain. If the clinician who prescribed the medication is available, beneficiaries can ask them to call in a new prescription to any network pharmacy.

As a reminder, TRICARE beneficiaries, other than active duty service members, may receive urgent care from any TRICARE-authorized urgent care center or provider and do not need a referral. This allows beneficiaries to seek nonemergency care for illnesses or injuries if their primary care provider is unavailable because of emergencies. Any TRICARE beneficiary who reasonably believes they have an emergency should always call 911 or, go to the nearest emergency room.

Beneficiaries are advised to visit Express Scripts’ https://militaryrx.express-scripts.com/notices/weather/2026-jul-27/state-emergency-alert-grasshopper-fire-oregon for updates.

###

The Defense Health Agency provides health services to 9.5 million beneficiaries, including uniformed service members, military retirees, and their families. AUGUSTA, Ga (WJBF) – A proposal from the Defense Health Agency came earlier this year for the Eisenhower Army Medical Center to be downgraded to an ambulatory care facility. The change would transition emergency care to urgent care, with the facility moving away from inpatient service.

Representative Rick Allen of Georgia’s 12th District is against the decision to downgrade Eisenhower. The National Defense Authorization Act for the 2027 fiscal year passed in the House of Representatives on July 22nd. Representative Allen included a provision in the bill to help prevent the center from changing its service.

Representative Allen said there was a companion bill in the Senate, but it failed to move forward. Both Georgia Senators voted against that bill progressing. The Senate now has the House version of the bill to consider.

Representative Allen said the issue impacts more than just his district. The Eisenhower Army Medical Center serves beyond just Augusta in the CSRA.

title: TRICARE For Life + Medicare in South Carolina: What Military Retirees Must Do at 65
authors: Ben J. Mauldin, Jennifer Mauldin, Ben Mauldin
description:
What happens to TRICARE at 65 When you become eligible for Medicare (usually at 65), your TRICARE doesn't disappear — it transforms into TRICARE For Life (TFL).
To keep TRICARE after 65, you must enroll in Medicare Part B. TRICARE will not waive it.
Always confirm your specific situation with TRICARE, Medicare (1-800-MEDICARE), or a licensed agent.
To keep TRICARE (which becomes TRICARE For Life) after 65, most military retirees must enroll in Medicare Part B and pay the premium — $202.90 a month in 2026 for most people.
TRICARE For Life applies to each person individually, so your spouse must enroll in Medicare Part B when they turn 65 to keep their own TRICARE For Life coverage.
text:
If you're a military retiree, TRICARE has probably been the easiest part of your life for decades. Then you approach 65, the Medicare mail starts arriving, and suddenly there are deadlines, premiums, and a dozen companies telling you to buy things.

Here's the honest version, from someone who helps South Carolina veterans through this every year. At 65, two things are true: there's one Medicare step you absolutely cannot skip — and there's a whole shelf of coverage you're being pitched that you probably don't need. Getting both of those right is the entire game.

What happens to TRICARE at 65

When you become eligible for Medicare (usually at 65), your TRICARE doesn't disappear — it transforms into TRICARE For Life (TFL). TFL is excellent coverage: it wraps around Original Medicare and pays as your secondary insurance. Medicare pays first, TFL picks up most of what's left. For most retirees, the combination leaves very little out of pocket.

But TFL only works if you hold up your side of the deal — and that side is Medicare.

The one step you cannot skip: Medicare Part B

This is the part that costs veterans dearly when they miss it. To keep TRICARE after 65, you must enroll in Medicare Part B. TRICARE will not waive it.

Three things to burn into memory:

The premium. Part B costs $202.90 a month in 2026 for most people (higher earners pay more — see IRMAA below).

The consequence of skipping it. If you don't enroll in Medicare when you're supposed to, your TRICARE benefits end — as early as the first day of the month you turn 65. This isn't a warning; it's the rule.

The penalty for being late. Miss your enrollment window and Medicare adds a 10% penalty to your Part B premium for every 12 months you could have had it but didn't — and that penalty sticks for life.

Your enrollment window is a 7-month Initial Enrollment Period: the 3 months before your 65th-birthday month, the birthday month itself, and the 3 months after. Don't wait until the end of it — enroll early so your coverage is active the day you need it.

(Also make sure you're enrolled in Medicare Part A, which most retirees get premium-free based on their work record. There's no reason to skip it.)

Now the good news: what you can SKIP

Here's what almost no one tells veterans, and where I often save people money instead of selling them something. Because TRICARE For Life is so strong, you generally do not need the extra products aimed at other Medicare beneficiaries:

You don't need a Medigap (Medicare Supplement) plan. TFL already does the job a Medigap does — it wraps around Original Medicare and covers most of the cost-sharing. Buying a Medigap on top is usually paying twice for the same protection.

You don't need a Medicare Part D drug plan. The TRICARE pharmacy benefit is "creditable" prescription coverage — Medicare considers it at least as good as Part D. That means you're already covered and you're protected from the Part D late-enrollment penalty, so you can decline Part D with confidence.

You generally don't need a Medicare Advantage plan. Enrolling in one can actually complicate how TFL coordinates. For most retirees, Original Medicare + TFL is the cleanest, strongest setup.

So if someone is pushing you toward a supplement, a drug plan, or an Advantage plan "because you're turning 65," pump the brakes. A good agent's job here is to confirm you're set — not to sell you a fourth layer you don't need.

What to Do Two moves, in order: (1) Enroll in Medicare Part A and Part B during your 7-month window so TRICARE For Life switches on smoothly. (2) Skip the Medigap and Part D pitches — TFL already covers those roles. If you want a second set of eyes to confirm before your birthday, that's exactly what I'm here for, and it's free.

Two things higher earners and couples should know

IRMAA. If your income is above certain thresholds, Medicare adds an income-related surcharge (IRMAA) to your Part B premium — so your cost can be higher than $202.90. It's based on your tax return from a couple of years back, and it's worth planning for.

Your spouse has their own deadline. TRICARE For Life follows each person individually. Your spouse must enroll in Medicare Part B when they turn 65 to keep their own TFL coverage. Don't let one birthday get handled and the other slip.

A note on exceptions

Most retirees must take Part B at 65 — full stop. But a few situations differ (for example, if you're still on active duty past 65, or covered as the family member of an active-duty service member). If that's you, confirm your timing directly with TRICARE before you make any decision. When in doubt, ask.

South Carolina is full of people this affects

South Carolina is home to hundreds of thousands of veterans and a heavy active-and-retired military presence — Shaw Air Force Base in Sumter, MCAS Beaufort in the Lowcountry, and Fort Jackson in Columbia, among others. That means a lot of neighbors are hitting this exact 65th-birthday decision every month, and a lot of them are getting bad or salesy advice.

You don't have to navigate it alone, and you should never pay for help choosing Medicare coverage. Free, trustworthy help is available through 1-800-MEDICARE, the TRICARE line, South Carolina's SHIP counselors, and a local licensed agent like me. If you're closer to the Midlands, I go deeper on the base angle in Military Retirees Near Fort Jackson: TRICARE For Life and Medicare, and you can always reach local Medicare help in the Columbia area.

Turning 65 with TRICARE? Let's Confirm You're Set — for Free.

No-cost, no-pressure review for military retirees. I'll make sure your Part B timing is right so TRICARE For Life switches on cleanly — and I'll tell you honestly what you don't need to buy.

📞 Call or Text Ben: 803-920-8827 🌐 MauldinInsuranceGroup.com 📍 100 Old Cherokee Rd STE F #167, Lexington, SC · Serving all of South Carolina · Thank you for your service.

This article is general information, not enrollment advice. Always confirm your specific situation with TRICARE, Medicare (1-800-MEDICARE), or a licensed agent.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do military retirees have to enroll in Medicare Part B at 65? Yes. To keep TRICARE (which becomes TRICARE For Life) after 65, most military retirees must enroll in Medicare Part B and pay the premium — $202.90 a month in 2026 for most people. If you don't enroll when eligible, your TRICARE coverage can end.

What happens if I skip Medicare Part B? Skipping Part B can end your TRICARE benefits as early as the first day of the month you turn 65, and Medicare adds a lifelong late-enrollment penalty of 10% of the Part B premium for every 12 months you delayed. It's a costly mistake to avoid.

Do I need a Medigap plan if I have TRICARE For Life? Generally no. TRICARE For Life already wraps around Original Medicare and covers most cost-sharing, functioning much like a Medigap plan. Buying a separate Medicare Supplement is usually paying twice for the same protection.

Do I need Medicare Part D if I have TRICARE For Life? No. The TRICARE pharmacy benefit is creditable prescription coverage — Medicare considers it at least as good as Part D — so you're already covered and protected from the Part D late penalty. You can add Part D later if you ever choose to, but most retirees don't need it.

Does my spouse also have to enroll in Medicare Part B? Yes. TRICARE For Life applies to each person individually, so your spouse must enroll in Medicare Part B when they turn 65 to keep their own TRICARE For Life coverage.

By SrA Jacob Hall, Louisiana Air National Guard Public Affairs Office

VOLK FIELD, Wis. – Airmen from the 159th Civil Engineering Squadron, Louisiana Air National Guard, constructed a fire training tower at Volk Field Combat Readiness Training Center in Camp Douglas, Wisconsin, during annual training July 13-24.

The project enhanced the squadron’s expeditionary construction capabilities while providing the Volk Field Fire Department with a permanent training facility to improve firefighter readiness and emergency response capabilities.

The 159th Civil Engineering Squadron is one of several Air National Guard civil engineering squadrons supporting the project. Each unit completes a portion of the construction before turning the project over to the next unit. The phased approach challenges Airmen to continue work started by another organization while strengthening interoperability and relationships among participating units.

The deployment also allowed Airmen to sharpen their technical skills in a field environment by planning, preparing and executing construction while operating heavy equipment. The hands-on experience mirrored real-world contingency operations and reinforced expeditionary readiness.

“The existing fire training tower at Volk Field is more than 30 years old and is scheduled for demolition, making this project a direct investment in a modern training facility where military firefighters can continue developing lifesaving skills,” said Master Sgt. Chad Grabert, 159th Civil Engineering Squadron base engineer emergency force manager. “In return, this mission has given our civil engineering Airmen an invaluable opportunity to apply their Air Force specialty code skills, learn new techniques and gain hands-on experience they may not receive at their home station.”

Beyond technical proficiency, the project reinforced teamwork and communication. Working together throughout the duty day and building camaraderie after hours strengthened relationships that contributed to mission success.

“We worked together as a team, and I learned how important communication is,” said Airman 1st Class Angel Rodriguez De Leon, 159th Civil Engineering Squadron structural journeyman. “This mission gave me the opportunity to learn skills I normally wouldn’t get to practice during a drill weekend. Some of my biggest lessons came after work, just talking with everyone over dinner and learning from the experience of the people around me.”

The project demonstrated the 159th Civil Engineering Squadron’s ability to deliver lasting infrastructure while increasing the readiness, experience and proficiency of its Airmen.

KISSIMMEE, Fla.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- PVP Labs, a clinical-stage biotechnology company advancing peptide-based therapeutics, today announced that research on Taphalgin® (Lumekefamide) has been selected for oral presentation at the 2026 Military Health System Research Symposium (MHSRS), a premier scientific forum focused on the unique medical needs of deployed Warfighters.

Joseph Stauffer, D.O., MBA, FAPCR, Chief Medical Officer of PVP Labs, will present the company's research on Taphalgin as a promising and much-needed battlefield pain-control solution. The presentation will highlight its rapid onset, effective analgesia, dual mechanism of action, extensive clinical experience, and confirmed non-scheduled status while in development.

Taphalgin is a first-in-class tetrapeptide analgesic engineered to deliver rapid, clinically meaningful pain relief while avoiding many of the traditional liabilities associated with conventional opioids. Its dual mechanism of action combines highly selective μ1-opioid receptor agonism with calcium-channel modulation, preserving strong analgesic efficacy while supporting a potentially improved safety and operational profile.

Advancing non-addictive pain treatments is an established military medical priority. U.S. military research programs are actively pursuing novel drug alternatives for battlefield pain control that can preserve physiological and cognitive performance at the point of care. PVP Labs believes Taphalgin is directly aligned with these goals.

"Battlefield medicine urgently needs an analgesic that can act rapidly and effectively without adding unnecessary respiratory, cognitive, or logistical burdens," said Eugene Zabolotsky, CEO of PVP Labs. "Taphalgin combines novel peptide design, extensive human experience, and confirmed non-scheduled status. We believe it represents a much-needed potential solution for Warfighters injured in combat and treated in austere environments."

Taphalgin® Clinical and Military Highlights

Rapid, effective pain relief: Onset of clinically meaningful analgesia in approximately 15-30 minutes.

Dual-mechanism innovation: Selective μ1-opioid receptor agonism and calcium-channel modulation.

Extensive clinical experience: Evaluated across six clinical trials and supported by more than 100,000 documented human exposures with no recorded evidence of euphoria, addiction, or respiratory depression events.

Confirmed non-scheduled status: The DEA determined that Lumekefamide is not a controlled substance or listed chemical under the Controlled Substances Act while in development.

Aligned with military priorities: A potential non-addictive drug alternative for battlefield pain control without physiological or cognitive impairment.

Taphalgin® (Lumekefamide) is a novel investigational tetrapeptide analgesic currently under regulatory development in the United States and has not been approved by the FDA.

title: What Does TRICARE Cover? Full Benefits & Exclusions Guide - Military.com
description:
Understanding what TRICARE covers, and what TRICARE exclusions exist, can save families thousands of dollars and a lot of frustration.
What Does TRICARE Cover?
The cost of TRICARE for military families varies depending on your TRICARE plan and military status.
Additionally, mental health care, dental care, and specialty care can be limited in remote overseas postings.
Before you see a healthcare provider, make sure to call ahead to verify that your TRICARE plan is accepted.
text:
Military families often discover TRICARE's limitations at the worst possible time: when a child needs braces, a spouse starts therapy, or a veteran wants to try acupuncture for back pain.

TRICARE exclusions aren't a secret, but they're often buried in the fine print that most people never read until they get a bill. Understanding what TRICARE covers, and what TRICARE exclusions exist, can save families thousands of dollars and a lot of frustration.

What Does TRICARE Cover?

TRICARE is the federal health insurance program for active duty service members, retirees, and their eligible dependents. Depending on the TRICARE plan you're enrolled in, you'll have access to a broad range of medical services, such as:

Preventive care: Annual physicals, vaccines, well-child visits, and cancer screenings.

Inpatient and outpatient care: Hospitalizations, surgeries, emergency room visits, and specialist appointments.

Maternity care: Prenatal visits, labor and delivery, and postpartum follow-up.

Mental health care: Inpatient and outpatient psychiatric care and substance use treatment.

Prescription drugs: Covered through the TRICARE Pharmacy Program, with access to military pharmacies, retail pharmacies, and the TRICARE mail-order program.

Durable medical equipment: Wheelchairs, crutches, prosthetics, and orthotics when medically necessary.

Lab and diagnostic services: Blood work, imaging (X-rays, MRIs, CT scans), and pathology.

What Does TRICARE Not Cover?

TRICARE excludes a number of services, and it only covers treatment that’s considered "medically necessary.” Some of the most common TRICARE exclusions include:

Cosmetic and elective procedures: Rhinoplasty, liposuction, hair restoration, and eyelid surgery for appearance are not covered. Even reconstructive surgery can be denied if TRICARE deems it cosmetic.

Routine dental care: Standard cleanings, fillings, and orthodontics for dependents are excluded from most TRICARE plans.

Routine vision care: Eye exams for glasses and contact lenses, frames, and contacts are not covered under standard TRICARE.

Hearing aids: TRICARE covers diagnosis and treatment of hearing conditions, but generally doesn't cover hearing aids for adult dependents.

Custodial care: Long-term care in a nursing home or assisted living facility that is primarily for help with daily activities, not skilled nursing, is excluded.

Most alternative therapies: Acupuncture, naturopathic medicine, massage therapy, and homeopathy are largely excluded, with limited exceptions.

Weight loss programs: Bariatric surgery and medically supervised weight loss programs are typically not covered unless specific criteria are met.

TRICARE Out-of-Pocket Costs

TRICARE is one of the most affordable health care options for military families, but it’s only free if you’re on active duty. The cost of TRICARE for military families varies depending on your TRICARE plan and military status.

Does TRICARE Include Dental Coverage?

Standard TRICARE plans don’t include dental coverage for dependents (active duty service members receive dental care through military treatment facilities). Families who want dental coverage can enroll in the TRICARE Dental Program (TDP), which covers:

Routine cleanings

X-rays

Fillings

Root canals

Oral surgery

Tooth extractions

Crowns

Dentures

Braces and orthodontia

Does TRICARE Cover Vision?

TRICARE doesn’t cover routine vision care, like eye exams or contact lenses, for any plan member. Active duty service members can access optometry services at military treatment facilities for readiness-related exams, but dependents and retirees are largely on their own.

Does TRICARE Cover Therapy?

TRICARE covers mental health and substance use treatment, including individual therapy, group therapy, inpatient psychiatric care, and medication management. Under TRICARE Prime, there are no copays for mental health visits at military facilities, and small copays for network civilian providers.

However, there are limitations for therapy coverage under TRICARE:

Provider availability: Finding a TRICARE-accepting therapist in many parts of the country is difficult. TRICARE's reimbursement rates are lower than many private insurers, so a significant number of licensed therapists don't participate in the network. This can mean long waits or driving significant distances for covered care.

Out-of-network costs: If you see a therapist who doesn't accept TRICARE, you'll pay out-of-pocket. TRICARE Select will reimburse a portion for non-network providers, but Prime will not.

Marriage counseling: Couples therapy is covered when at least one partner has a diagnosable mental health condition being treated. Voluntary marital counseling without a clinical diagnosis is generally not covered.

Are Experimental Treatments and Alternative Care Covered?

TRICARE applies a strict "medically necessary and proven effective" standard. That means experimental and alternative treatments are often excluded by default. This includes:

Acupuncture (with limited exceptions)

Chiropractic care beyond what's authorized at specific military facilities

Naturopathy and homeopathy

Most herbal or nutritional supplements

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy for most conditions

Experimental cancer treatments not yet approved by the FDA

One exception is clinical trials, which TRICARE does cover, as long as the trial is approved.

Does TRICARE Work Overseas?

TRICARE does work overseas, which is good news for service members and their families who want help paying for military healthcare costs abroad.

Active duty service members stationed overseas are automatically enrolled in TRICARE Prime Overseas, which provides coverage through the regional contractor.

Active duty family members, retirees, and eligible dependants living overseas can enroll in the TRICARE Select Overseas plan.

Retired National Guard and Reserve members under age 60 can get the TRICARE Retired Reserve Overseas plan, which also covers their family members.

These TRICARE plans cover emergency care anywhere in the world without prior authorization. For planned care, however, you must use TRICARE-authorized providers or get prior authorization for planned care. Typically, you pay upfront and submit a claim for reimbursement.

It’s important to consider that in some locations, the nearest TRICARE-authorized provider may be hours away, so finding care overseas isn't always easy. Additionally, mental health care, dental care, and specialty care can be limited in remote overseas postings.

Supplemental Health Insurance Options for Military Families

If you want coverage for TRICARE coverage gaps, you might consider a supplemental insurance plan for the military. Here are some of the most common options that families choose:

TRICARE Supplement Plans: Some private insurers offer TRICARE supplement plans that cover cost shares, deductibles, and some excluded services. Monthly premiums depend on age and plan, and they're most valuable for families on TRICARE Select who have higher cost shares.

TRICARE Dental Program (TDP): TDP is the official dental add-on plan, which is administered by United Concordia. It covers routine and preventative dental care in the U.S. and overseas.

Commercial vision plans: If you want coverage for eye exams and glasses, you can consider enrolling in a standalone vision insurance plan from a provider like VSP or EyeMed. These plans aren’t affiliated with TRICARE.

FEDVIP (Federal Employees Dental and Vision Insurance Program): Some TRICARE-eligible individuals can also access FEDVIP, which offers competitive dental and vision options through a federal marketplace.

FSAs and HSAs: Active duty families can’t use health savings accounts (HSAs), but some retirees on high-deductible plans can. Flexible spending accounts (FSAs) through a spouse's civilian employer can also help offset TRICARE cost shares and excluded expenses.

FAQ

Q: Does TRICARE cover pre-existing conditions?

Yes. TRICARE covers pre-existing conditions for all eligible plan members. Coverage begins when eligibility begins, with no waiting periods for pre-existing health issues.

Q: Can military spouses keep TRICARE after a divorce?

No, military spouses lose TRICARE eligibility after divorce unless they meet the "20/20/20 rule": the service member served at least 20 years, the marriage lasted at least 20 years, and the two periods overlap by at least 20 years. Those who don't qualify can purchase a temporary continuation of coverage for up to 36 months (called Transitional Survivor Coverage) but must pay full premiums.

Q: Does TRICARE cover weight loss surgery?

Bariatric surgery is covered under TRICARE, but it comes with strict criteria. You must have a BMI of 40 or higher (or 35+ with serious comorbid conditions), documentation of failed conventional weight loss attempts, psychological evaluation, and approval from a TRICARE-authorized bariatric program.

Q: What happens to TRICARE coverage when a service member separates?

Service members who separate before reaching 20 years of qualifying service lose TRICARE eligibility within 60 to 180 days, depending on their length of service. They may be eligible for a temporary continuation called the Continued Health Care Benefit Program (CHCBP) for up to 18 months. However, the premiums are typically very expensive.

Q: Is TRICARE accepted everywhere?

Two healthcare and academic leaders have joined the Thomas Jefferson University (TJU) Board of Trustees to help advance its mission of improving lives

PHILADELPHIA, July 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Jefferson (which includes Thomas Jefferson University, Jefferson Health, and Jefferson Health Plans) announced today the appointment of Anthony P. Monaco, MD, PhD, and Elizabeth Bierbower to its enterprise (TJU) Board of Trustees.

Dr. Anthony P. (Tony) Monaco is an internationally recognized geneticist and academic leader best known for his groundbreaking discovery of the gene responsible for X-linked Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies, a milestone that transformed human genetics and enabled new therapeutic approaches.

He spent more than two decades at the University of Oxford, where he became Professor of Human Genetics and directed the Wellcome Trust Centre for Human Genetics, expanding its global impact in neurogenetics research. He also served as Pro-Vice-Chancellor, helping guide Oxford's academic and strategic growth.

In 2011, Dr. Monaco became the 13th President of Tufts University, leading the institution for 12 years. His presidency was marked by major initiatives including the integration of the School of the Museum of Fine Arts, expanded commitments to diversity and inclusion, strengthened student mental health support, and university-wide sustainability efforts. He now serves as President Emeritus and University Professor, continuing his research in neurodevelopmental genetics and contributing to leading scientific and philanthropic organizations.

Elizabeth (Beth) Bierbower is a seasoned healthcare executive with more than 30 years of leadership experience across Commercial, Medicare Advantage, and TRICARE. She is recognized for driving strategic growth, advancing value-based care models, and leveraging innovation and partnerships to scale complex organizations.

At Humana, Beth served as Segment President and a member of the Executive Management Team, where she built a new division focused on transforming the Medicare Advantage customer experience. Previously, as President of the Group and Specialty Segment, she led a $7B business serving 11 million members and oversaw Humana's successful award of the $40B TRICARE contract—the largest in military healthcare history.

She also held senior roles as Chief Operating Officer of Specialty Benefits and Enterprise Vice President for Product Development and Innovation at Humana, as well as leadership positions at Highmark Blue Cross Blue Shield and Coventry Health Plans. Known for operational discipline and innovation, Beth has consistently delivered profitable growth while fostering talent development and advancing industry-leading capabilities.

"On behalf of the Thomas Jefferson University Board of Trustees, I am pleased to welcome Dr. Anthony Monaco and Beth Bierbower to the Board. Tony's internationally recognized contributions to genetic research, combined with his distinguished leadership in higher education, reflect a deep commitment to advancing discovery, innovation and student success. Beth brings decades of healthcare leadership experience and a proven track record of driving growth, improving the patient and member experience, and advancing innovative models of care. Together, their expertise and perspectives will be invaluable as we continue to strengthen Jefferson's mission of improving lives through excellence in patient care, education, research and population health," said Michael E. Sneed, Chair, Thomas Jefferson University Board of Trustees.

Recognition of Retiring TJU Board Members

The TJU Board of Trustees also recognizes the extraordinary service of two retiring members whose leadership has left a lasting mark on the University. Among them is Patricia D. Wellenbach, who served on the Board from May 2015 through June 2026. In July 2021, she was appointed Chair of the Board of Trustees, becoming both the first nurse and the first woman to hold this distinguished role in Jefferson's history since its founding in 1824.

Throughout her tenure, Ms. Wellenbach was a steadfast champion of Jefferson's mission to improve lives through reimagining health, education, and discovery. Her remarkable leadership, strategic insight, and collaborative approach helped guide the institution through a period of significant growth and transformation, advancing Jefferson's vision and strengthening its impact across the communities it serves.

John J. Fung, MD, PhD, served on the Board of Trustees from July 2023 through June 2026 with exceptional integrity, dedication, and purpose. A renowned physician, researcher, and academic leader, Dr. Fung brought invaluable clinical expertise and strategic insight into the Board's work. His independent physician perspective strengthened oversight of one of Jefferson's highest priorities: delivering outstanding patient care. Throughout his service, Dr. Fung provided thoughtful counsel and a depth of expertise that enriched Board discussions and informed key decisions. His contributions have had a meaningful and lasting impact on the Board and the institution.

"I want to express my sincere gratitude to Patricia Wellenbach and Dr. John Fung for their dedicated service to our Board of Trustees. Trish's historic leadership as Board Chair helped guide Jefferson through a period of tremendous growth and transformation. John brought invaluable clinical expertise and counsel that strengthened our focus on delivering exceptional patient care. We are deeply grateful for their contributions and lasting impact on Jefferson, and we thank them for their years of service and stewardship," said Joseph G. Cacchione, MD, Chief Executive Officer, Jefferson.

Headshots are available for download here.

About Jefferson

Jefferson is reimagining health care and higher education to create unparalleled value throughout Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware. More than 65,000 people strong, Jefferson is dedicated to providing high-quality, compassionate clinical care for patients; making our communities healthier and stronger; preparing tomorrow's professional leaders for 21st-century careers; and creating new knowledge through basic/programmatic, clinical and applied research. Thomas Jefferson University, home of Sidney Kimmel Medical College, Jefferson College of Nursing, the College of Business, the College of Fashion & Textiles, and the College of Architecture, Design & Engineering, dates back to 1824 and today comprises 11 colleges and one school offering 200+ undergraduate and graduate programs to more than 8,700 students. Jefferson Health, nationally ranked as one of the top 15 not-for-profit healthcare systems in the country and the largest provider in the Philadelphia and Lehigh Valley areas, serves patients through millions of encounters each year at 33 hospital campuses and more than 700 outpatient and urgent care locations throughout the region. Jefferson Health Plans, through Health Partners Plans Inc., is a not-for-profit managed healthcare organization offering a broad range of health coverage options to more than 370,000 members for more than 40 years.

The company will present two scientific posters exploring applications of its transcutaneous auricular neurostimulation (tAN®) platform for cognitive performance and sleep in operational and military health contexts.

Michael Darrow, PhD, Spark's Director of Research Innovations, will present "Enhancing Warfighter Readiness with Wearable Auricular Neurostimulation: Development and Clinical Evaluation." Navid Khodaparast, PhD, Spark's Chief Science Officer will present "Anxiety and Sleep in first responders: Wearable Auricular Neurostimulation to Improve Stress Resilience and Sleep in First Responders: Decentralized Clinical Trial Results" The poster will demonstrate how daily tAN® sessions in first responders can significantly reduce anxiety, improve sleep quality, and overall wellbeing.

MHSRS is the Department of Defense's premier scientific conference dedicated to military medical research, bringing together military, federal, and civilian researchers to advance the health and readiness of service members. Spark's presence at MHSRS reflects a strategic expansion of its tAN® platform beyond clinical and consumer settings into the military-ready space, extending the company's research base to the operational demands of service members and first responders.

"Readiness starts with resilience," said Navid Khodaparast, PhD, Chief Science Officer of Spark Biomedical. "Our research demonstrates how non-invasive auricular neurostimulation may help reduce stress, improve sleep, and support the health and performance of service members and first responders."

title: Unlock your health by understanding the TRICARE Prime referral process - DVIDS

text:
Do you have TRICARE Prime? If so, you likely get most of your routine healthcare from your primary care manager. But sometimes, you may need specialty care that your PCM can’t provide. This is when your PCM will give you a referral. Having a referral can reduce your out-of-pocket expenses. Referrals can also help reduce the time you need to wait to get specialty care.

“If you have TRICARE Prime, referrals are important because they help you get the right care from the right providers,” said Jacob Sanchez, referral management subject expert, TRICARE Health Plan, at the Defense Health Agency. “Knowing how they work makes it easier to access the services you need and get the most out of your TRICARE benefit.”

In this article, you’ll learn about the TRICARE Prime referral process.

How referrals work

Your provider starts the process by sending a referral request to your regional contractor. They review the referral request and, once processed, send you a notification in your beneficiary self-service portal. Then, you can contact the provider listed on the notification letter to make your appointment.

When to get a referral

Do you need a referral? It depends on your beneficiary category, your TRICARE plan, and the type of care you need.

**Active duty service members:**You need a referral for any nonemergency care your PCM doesn’t provide. This includes specialty care and urgent care. If you get care without a referral, you may have to pay out of pocket.

All others with a TRICARE Prime plan: You don’t need a referral for preventive care, urgent care, or most outpatient mental healthcare. You do need a referral for specialty care and some diagnostic services, as described in the TRICARE Plans Overview Fact Sheet. If you get this care without a referral, you’ll be using the http://www.tricare.mil/pointofservice. You’ll pay more out of pocket if you use this option.

TRICARE For Life: You don’t need a referral for most healthcare services. But you may need pre-authorization for certain services.

You don’t need a referral to get emergency care. However, you should contact your PCM the next business day after you get emergency care.

Other helpful referral tips

Second opinions

Do you have concerns or questions after seeing a specialist for care? Are you unsure about a diagnosis or treatment option? You have the right to request a second opinion. With TRICARE Prime, you should request a second opinion through your PCM.

Referrals expire

Don’t forget that referrals have expiration dates. Make sure to schedule your appointment and get care before your referral expires. You can find the expiration date on your notification letter. If your referral expires and you need a new one, contact your PCM. When you get a referral for specialty care, you can expect to get an appointment within 28 days.

Transferring referrals within and between regions

Are youmoving to another locationin the U.S.? Whether your sponsor has recently gotten permanent change of station orders, or you’re moving for personal reasons—there’s good news about moving with your TRICARE coverage. Your active referrals remain valid within the same region and automatically transfer between the East and West Region.

If you’re moving to a different region:

Do you have any active referrals? Your referrals will still be valid in your new location. Your active referrals will automatically transfer to your new contractor once you change your enrollment and update the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System with your new address. Here are the steps you should follow:

After your move, update your enrollment within 90 days. Log in to milConnect and choose Beneficiary Web Enrollment from the Benefits menu. Update your enrollment based on your new address, so that DEERS shows that you’re in your new location

Contact your new regional contractor. Ask them to create a new specialty referral in your new location for the active specialty referrals that were transferred. This will help you continue your specialty care without delay.

Your new contractor will generate new specialty referrals to a new specialty provider. This new referral will be based on your location, specialty you were referred to, episode of care, and the expiration date of your original referral.(**Note:**Your specialty referral may be assigned to a military hospital or clinic in your new location, if the military hospital or clinic is able to provide the care.)

Call to schedule an appointment with the new specialty provider’s office.

Call your new PCM to schedule an appointment. (Note: The referral transfer process is meant to avoid delays for specialty care while waiting to establish care with your PCM for new referrals. You should make an appointment with your new PCM as soon as possible.)

Contact your regional contractor with questions about referrals:

West Region: 888-TRIWEST (874-9378)

East Region: 800-444-5445

If you’re moving within the same region:

After your move, update your enrollment within 90 days. Log in to http://milconnect.dmdc.osd.mil/milconnect/ and choose Beneficiary Web Enrollment from the Benefits menu. Your update will trigger the DMDC/DEERS Support Office to notify your regional contractor about your address change. NOTE: If you need help, contact your regional contractor.

Call your regional contractor. Ask them to create a new specialty referral in your new location, to see a new specialist. (**Note:**Your specialty referral may be assigned to a military hospital or clinic in your new location, if the military hospital or clinic is able to provide the care.)

text:
Teleflex Incorporated (NYSE: TFX) has received Biologics License Application approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for EZPLAZ™ Freeze Dried Plasma, which the company claims is the first freeze dried plasma product licensed by the FDA.

The product is indicated for transfusion in adults with bleeding-related conditions requiring replacement of plasma coagulation factors, including uncontrolled bleeding, when plasma is required and other plasma products are not available.

According to Teleflex, EZPLAZ™ uses a patented flexible plastic bag rather than the glass bottles used by existing freeze dried plasma products currently authorized under Emergency Use Authorization. The product has a storage temperature of 2 to 25°C, a 12-month shelf life, and can be reconstituted in approximately one to 2.5 minutes.

Teleflex entered a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement in April 2014 with the Defense Health Agency's Warfighter Protection and Acute Care program to develop the product. The Defense Health Agency had identified an FDA-approved, commercially available freeze dried plasma as a medical priority for battlefield use.

"EZPLAZ™ FDP can potentially enable the transfusion of plasma in situations where it is critically needed, including air and road ambulances, in the hospital, and on the battlefield," said Jake Newman, President and General Manager, Global Vascular and Emergency Medicine at Teleflex.

The product carries safety risks common to blood-derived products, including hemolytic transfusion reactions, transfusion-related acute lung injury, hypersensitivity reactions, and the potential transmission of infectious agents. It is contraindicated in patients with a history of hypersensitivity to plasma-derived products and in patients with IgA deficiency.

text:
MOAA’s message to a Senate panel scrutinizing the TRICARE Pharmacy Program stressed the need to preserve affordable access to medications, rebuild the brick-and-mortar pharmacy network, and restore coverage for GLP-1 medications to TRICARE For Life (TFL) users.

Senate Armed Services Personnel subcommittee members scrutinized terms of the fifth-generation pharmacy contract, referred to as TPharm5, during the July 15 hearing and emphasized the importance of robust access to affordable prescription medications for servicemembers and retirees, as well as their families and survivors.

In its statement for the record (SFR), MOAA expressed appreciation for the committee’s oversight and urged Congress to strengthen protections for beneficiaries as pharmacy policies continue to evolve.

“Broad pharmacy access, comprehensive medication coverage, and affordable copays have long been hallmarks of the TRICARE Pharmacy Program, but these core benefits have suffered steady erosion in recent years,” MOAA wrote. “While MOAA acknowledges the need for cost containment, any pharmacy reforms must preserve the high standard of access, coverage, and affordability that honors our nation’s commitment to those who serve.”

[MORE FROM THE HEARING: Senators Question Whether Military Pharmacy Program Is the Best Deal for Beneficiaries]

Subcommittee leadership acknowledged concerns that changes to the pharmacy benefit can have negative implications for military families. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the subcommittee’s ranking member, noted that “the consequences of losing access to your local pharmacy can be immeasurable,” reflecting concerns raised by beneficiaries affected by TRICARE retail pharmacy network reductions.

Subcommittee Chairman Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) emphasized the need to balance fiscal responsibility with beneficiary access.

“We must strike the right balance between controlling costs and maintaining access,” Tuberville said. “Savings achieved on paper are not real savings if they result in delayed treatment, reduced readiness, or additional health care costs down the road.”

[READ: MOAA's Statement for the Record]

MOAA’s SFR outlined four key priorities for congressional oversight and legislative action:

Restore GLP-1 Coverage for TRICARE For Life

Reinstating TRICARE Pharmacy Program coverage of GLP-1 medications for eligible TFL beneficiaries remains one of MOAA’s top legislative priorities. MOAA urged Congress to ensure the Defense Health Agency (DHA) has the statutory authority and appropriations necessary to reverse the 2025 policy change.

MOAA has seen extraordinary levels of engagement from both impacted patients who have lost GLP-1 coverage and other beneficiaries who fear future cuts to the retiree health care benefit. More than 800 TRICARE beneficiaries have contacted MOAA to share their feedback on the decision to revoke coverage of certain GLP-1 drugs from TFL beneficiaries.

[TAKE ACTION: Restore TRICARE For Life Coverage of GLP-1 Medications]

MOAA’s statement noted the inequity this policy creates between TFL and TRICARE Prime and Select coverage, the inconsistency with statutory guidance for the TRICARE Pharmacy Program, and the negative impact on beneficiaries.

We also noted TFL policy is out of step with Medicare efforts to expand access to affordable GLP-1s through the Medicare Bridge program.

[RELATED: New Medicare GLP-1 Program Excludes TRICARE For Life Beneficiaries]

Ensure Access to Medically Necessary Medications

MOAA urged Congress to ensure DHA implements a medical necessity review process for medications placed in TRICARE’s Tier 4 (Non-Covered) category.

Although Congress directed DHA to establish such a process in Senate report language accompanying the FY 2022 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), beneficiaries have no mechanism to request a medical necessity review for a Tier 4 medication when other formulary alternatives have failed.

Instituting such an exception process would bring TRICARE in line with commercial health plan benchmarks – such as the Blue Cross and Blue Shield Service Benefit Plan, better known as FEP Blue – while protecting military families with unique medical needs.

Restore the TRICARE Retail Pharmacy Network

The SFR renewed MOAA’s call to restore the retail pharmacy network after reductions under TPharm5 significantly narrowed beneficiary access and choice.

While additional pharmacies have been added since the initial cuts, it remains well below its pre-TPharm5 size.

[RELATED: Find a Network Pharmacy Near You]

MOAA successfully advocated for an independent review of the network cuts during our 2023 Advocacy in Action event. The resulting Government Accountability Office report showed at least 380,000 beneficiaries lost a pharmacy they had recently used while 98,000 beneficiaries were knocked out of distance-based access standards due to the network cuts. The narrowed network disproportionately affected elderly patients, rural residents, and beneficiaries with complex medical needs.

MOAA has called for greater transparency on savings generated by TPharm5, urging Congress to require DHA to distinguish between savings attributable to retail network reductions from those generated by other contract reforms, including specialty medication fulfillment.

Preserve Affordable Pharmacy Copays After 2027

DHA can adjust pharmacy copays beginning in 2028 without any requirement to consider prevailing commercial health plan cost-sharing practices or the impact of higher copayments on military beneficiaries. This creates the potential for disproportionate beneficiary copay increases on prescription medications.

MOAA is urging Congress to provide statutory guardrails on DHA authority to adjust pharmacy copays and protect beneficiaries from disproportionate copay increases in the future.

What’s Next

Unlike health care services that are used only occasionally or rarely, the pharmacy benefit is part of daily life for many. For this reason, even modest reductions in coverage, access, or affordability can have outsize effects on health outcomes, financial security, and confidence in the TRICARE program.

As Congress continues its oversight of the TRICARE Pharmacy Program, MOAA will continue to advocate for policies that preserve broad pharmacy access, medically appropriate coverage, and affordable cost-sharing so the program delivers on the health care benefit to those who have served and their families.

text:
A PCS. A marriage. The birth or adoption of a child. A return from activation. Retirement from military service. These milestones often come with long to-do lists, but one important decision that is easy to overlook is reviewing your TRICARE coverage.

Also Read: Free, flexible ideas to keep military kids engaged this summer

These changes may be recognized as a Qualifying Life Event (QLE) which provides eligible beneficiaries with a 90-day window to review and make certain changes to their TRICARE coverage outside of Open Season.

For families in the Tampa and Atlanta areas, that review may include the TRICARE Prime Demo by CareSource Military & Veterans.

The Department of Defense moves the households of approximately 300,000 service members and civilian employees each year. Many families arrive at a new duty station, unpack boxes and begin rebuilding their routines without realizing that a qualifying move may also open a new enrollment window.

“Most military families don’t realize that a PCS, marriage, new baby, retirement or other life change can create an opportunity to revisit their TRICARE coverage,” said Selene Martin, Associate Vice President of Market Strategy for CareSource Military & Veterans. “We want eligible beneficiaries to understand all of their options and choose the one that best supports their family’s needs during that season of life.”

Why Review Your Coverage After a Life Change?

A move may mean a new provider network. A new baby may bring different care needs. Retirement may change how a family accesses care. A plan that worked well six months ago may not fit the same way after circumstances change.

The QLE window gives eligible beneficiaries time to review whether their current coverage still meets their family’s needs.

It does not require a family to make a change. It gives them the opportunity to understand what is available before the 90-day period closes.

How Is the Demo Different From the TRICARE Prime Option You May Already Know?

Your underlying TRICARE benefits remain the same. What changes is the provider network and the organization helping coordinate your care.

For eligible beneficiaries who enroll, the TRICARE Prime Demo by CareSource Military & Veterans includes access to CareSource’s provider network, in-network specialist care without a referral, care coordination, telehealth and digital tools through the MyLife app.

Enrollment fees are also waived during the first year for eligible retirees and their family members. Prescription drug benefits continue through Express Scripts.

Those differences may be helpful if your family is reestablishing care after a move, managing ongoing specialist needs or preparing for retirement.

Before making a change, take time to look at your current providers, ongoing care needs and the kind of support your family may need next.

Understand the Window Before It Closes

A QLE does not automatically mean that changing plans is the right decision. It means eligible beneficiaries have a limited opportunity to review their options and decide what works best for their family.

For beneficiaries in Tampa and Atlanta who meet the eligibility requirements, that review may include the TRICARE Prime Demo by CareSource Military & Veterans.

To learn more about the Demo or check eligibility, visit CareSourceMilitary.com or call 1-833-230-2080.

title: Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound: Differences — and What the VA and Tricare Actually Cover
description:
The Two Drugs Behind Four Brand Names Semaglutide is the active ingredient in both Ozempic and Wegovy.
Completely different VA coverage pathways.
What Tricare Covers for Active-Duty Families Tricare is more permissive than the VA for weight-loss indications.
Tricare For Life and direct-care-only beneficiaries are excluded from weight-loss GLP-1 coverage as of Aug. 31, 2025.
Veterans with questions about their specific formulary coverage can call the VA pharmacy benefits line at 888-385-0235 or check the VA National Formulary at va.gov/formularyadvisor.
text:
Veterans asking their Department of Veterans Affairs health care provider about GLP-1 medications frequently run into a wall of brand names that seem interchangeable but are not — at least not for coverage purposes. Ozempic and Wegovy contain identical active ingredients. So do Mounjaro and Zepbound. But the VA treats them as categorically different drugs, and which one you can access depends on what is in your medical record.

Understanding the distinction is the single most important thing a veteran can do before walking into that appointment.

The Two Drugs Behind Four Brand Names

Semaglutide is the active ingredient in both Ozempic and Wegovy. Both are made by Novo Nordisk. Ozempic was FDA-approved for Type 2 diabetes management. Wegovy was approved for chronic weight management and, following a 2023 trial, for reducing major cardiovascular events in patients with established heart disease and obesity.

Same molecule. Different doses. Different FDA approvals. Completely different VA coverage pathways.

Tirzepatide works the same way. It is the active ingredient in both Mounjaro and Zepbound, both made by Eli Lilly. Mounjaro is FDA-approved for Type 2 diabetes. Zepbound is approved for obesity and, separately, for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea. Same molecule, different brand, different indication, different coverage.

Read More: A VA Clinic Gave Veterans GLP-1s for Weight Loss. A Year Later, Everything Improved

What the VA Actually Covers — By Diagnosis

The VA covers these drugs through its Meds by Mail program and at VA pharmacies, but the diagnosis in your record is the determining factor. Based on the VA's current formulary guidance as of mid-2026, here is the breakdown:

Veterans with a Type 2 diabetes diagnosis can access Ozempic and Mounjaro.

Veterans with an obstructive sleep apnea diagnosis can access Zepbound.

Veterans with a diagnosis for the prevention of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) — meaning established heart disease with obesity — can access Wegovy.

Veterans who want these drugs for weight loss without one of those specific diagnoses face a significantly harder path. VA classifies obesity medications as non-formulary except for documented medical necessity, and approval rates for weight-loss-only indications are low.

CHAMPVA — the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs — covers dependents of 100 percent permanently and totally disabled veterans; it does not cover GLP-1 medications for weight loss at all. CHAMPVA covers Ozempic and Mounjaro for Type 2 diabetes, Zepbound for sleep apnea, and Wegovy only for MACE prevention — the same diagnosis-driven structure as the VA but with no weight-loss pathway under any circumstances.

What Tricare Covers for Active-Duty Families

Tricare is more permissive than the VA for weight-loss indications. Tricare Prime, Select and premium-based plans cover Wegovy, Saxenda and Zepbound for weight management with prior authorization, provided the member meets body-mass-index criteria — 30 or above, or 27 or above with a weight-related comorbidity; has attempted lifestyle modification for at least six months; and has tried an oral weight-loss medication without success.

Tricare For Life and direct-care-only beneficiaries are excluded from weight-loss GLP-1 coverage as of Aug. 31, 2025. Meanwhile, however, Medicare introduced its Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program for $50 a month.

What Veterans Should Do Before Their Appointment

The most productive thing a veteran can do before discussing GLP-1 medications with their VA provider is to review their active diagnoses in their VA health record through MyHealtheVet and note whether Type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease or obstructive sleep apnea appears. If any of those diagnoses are present, the coverage pathway is clearer, and the conversation with the provider becomes simpler.

Read More: VA Study Finds Possible New Treatment for Melanoma, a Cancer Linked to Military Service

Veterans who want these medications for weight management without a qualifying diagnosis should ask their provider about enrollment in the VA's MOVE! weight management program. Documented participation in a structured lifestyle intervention strengthens the case for pharmacological treatment and is often a prerequisite in the VA's prior authorization process for weight-loss indications. The MOVE! program is free and available at all VA medical centers.

Veterans with questions about their specific formulary coverage can call the VA pharmacy benefits line at 888-385-0235 or check the VA National Formulary at va.gov/formularyadvisor.

title: Pentagon to test separate EMS reimbursement for prehospital blood - EMS1
authors: Sarah Roebuck, cinematic arts degree, sarah-roebuck
description:
It applies to authorized ground and air ambulance providers treating eligible military personnel, family members and retirees.
The project could also help determine whether separate reimbursement should become a permanent part of the TRICARE ambulance payment system.
Reimbursement cited as barrier to EMS blood programs Although military medical teams have used prehospital blood for years, the practice remains limited among civilian EMS agencies.
Prehospital blood transfusion qualifies a transport for the ALS2 rate, but the blood product itself is not reimbursed separately.
Would separate reimbursement for prehospital blood make your agency more likely to launch or expand a blood program?
text:
WASHINGTON — TRICARE, the Pentagon’s health insurance program, will test a new reimbursement model that pays civilian ambulance providers separately for blood administered before patients reach a hospital.

The Defense Health Agency, which oversees TRICARE for the Department of Defense, will launch the 5-year demonstration project on Jan. 1, 2027 and run through Dec. 31, 2031. It applies to authorized ground and air ambulance providers treating eligible military personnel, family members and retirees.

| MORE: EMS is more than a transportation service: Why reimbursement must evolve

Under the project, providers can receive an add-on payment for medically necessary whole blood, packed red blood cells, plasma or a combination of red blood cells and plasma administered during an ALS2, specialty care or air ambulance transport. Providers may also bill separately for the professional services involved in administering a transfusion.

The DHA said it will examine whether the reimbursement model improves outcomes for patients experiencing hemorrhagic shock, reduces overall healthcare costs and expands access to prehospital blood.

The project could also help determine whether separate reimbursement should become a permanent part of the TRICARE ambulance payment system.

Reimbursement cited as barrier to EMS blood programs

Although military medical teams have used prehospital blood for years, the practice remains limited among civilian EMS agencies.

Only about 1% to 2% of EMS agencies nationwide carry blood, according to America’s Blood Centers. Advocates say reimbursement is one of the largest barriers to starting and maintaining the programs.

Medicare and TRICARE generally reimburse ambulance services based on the level of care and transportation provided, with medical supplies included in the base payment. Prehospital blood transfusion qualifies a transport for the ALS2 rate, but the blood product itself is not reimbursed separately.

The DHA acknowledged that the additional ALS2 payment may not cover the cost of maintaining a prehospital blood program.

More than 70% of EMS agencies responding to a 2024 survey reported paying more than $500 per unit of blood, according to the Federal Register notice. More than one-third reported costs exceeding $800 per unit.

Those figures do not include all of the equipment, training and coordination required to keep blood available in ambulances. Agencies must closely monitor storage temperatures, train clinicians to administer the products, and coordinate with blood suppliers and hospitals to rotate unused units before they expire.

How ambulance providers will be paid

Under the demonstration, ambulance providers will be reimbursed at either the applicable hospital outpatient payment rate or the invoiced cost of the blood product, whichever is higher.

Providers that submit an invoice from a blood bank or supplier may receive reimbursement for the product’s actual cost. Those that do not submit an invoice will receive the hospital outpatient rate. Providers may also bill once per transport for transfusion administration services.

The add-on will apply to eligible patients covered by TRICARE Prime, TRICARE Select or TRICARE for Life, including those enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans. Claims outside the United States and its territories, along with cases in which another insurer is the primary payer, are excluded.

The DHA estimates the project will account for approximately $4.6 million in healthcare costs over 5 years, along with $100,000 in administrative expenses and $500,000 for evaluation.

The agency will review claims data during the project’s fifth year to determine whether the payment model improved outcomes, reduced costs and increased access to prehospital blood. The DHA may modify or end the project early if participation is limited or the reimbursement does not appear to meet those goals.

title: Medical device milestone: First FDA clearance for implant produced by point-of-care institution
authors: Clare Scott, Managing Editor - Manufacturing Group
description:
Advancing point-of-care manufacturing through collaboration This milestone represents the culmination of a multi-year collaboration between 3D Systems and 3D MAC to advance additive manufacturing (AM) in clinical environments.
“We believe point-of-care manufacturing is transforming the future of healthcare by bringing personalized medical devices closer to the patient.
The FDA clearance of the TCP System marks 3D MAC’s first-ever FDA-cleared medical device.
Industry leadership and future opportunities The clearance establishes multiple industry firsts, including the first FDA-cleared implant granted to a point-of-care institution and 3D MAC’s first FDA-cleared medical device.
It reinforces 3D Systems’ leadership in enabling point-of-care manufacturing and highlights its ability to help healthcare institutions navigate the path from concept through regulatory clearance and commercialization.
text:
The Defense Health Agency (DHA) and the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center’s 3D Medical Applications Center (3D MAC), with help from 3D Systems, achieved U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) premarket clearance for the 3D MAC Titanium Cranial Plate (TCP) System, the first-ever FDA-cleared implant granted to a point-of-care institution. 3D MAC's patient-specific TCP will be used to treat U.S. active duty personnel and war fighters suffering from traumatic head injuries around the world.

Advancing point-of-care manufacturing through collaboration

This milestone represents the culmination of a multi-year collaboration between 3D Systems and 3D MAC to advance additive manufacturing (AM) in clinical environments. The 3D Medical Applications Center, based at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, specializes in patient-specific anatomical models, surgical guides, and implants to support personalized care for service members and veterans.

“We believe point-of-care manufacturing is transforming the future of healthcare by bringing personalized medical devices closer to the patient. Our unique collaborations with the U.S. Defense Health Agency and the Department of Veterans Affairs underscore our leadership in this space and reinforce our commitment to expanding this business as a long-term growth driver for 3D Systems," says Jeff Graves, president and CEO of 3D Systems. Throughout the engagement, 3D Systems worked closely with 3D MAC to establish a robust quality management system (QMS) and provided support across the full development lifecycle, from design and validation through regulatory submission. The FDA clearance of the TCP System marks 3D MAC’s first-ever FDA-cleared medical device.

Enabling regulatory readiness and clinical innovation

3D Systems provided expertise in process controls, device design optimization, AM workflows, and regulatory strategy to support 3D MAC in achieving premarket clearance. This collaboration enabled the transition from concept to an FDA-cleared implant manufactured at the point-of-care.

“This clearance underscores the power of combining clinical innovation with deep expertise in additive manufacturing and regulatory compliance. We are honored to help enable expanded access to personalized care delivered at the point of treatment,” says Natalie Byrnes, manager of Product Development - Patient Specific Medical Technology, 3D Systems.

Industry leadership and future opportunities

The clearance establishes multiple industry firsts, including the first FDA-cleared implant granted to a point-of-care institution and 3D MAC’s first FDA-cleared medical device. It reinforces 3D Systems’ leadership in enabling point-of-care manufacturing and highlights its ability to help healthcare institutions navigate the path from concept through regulatory clearance and commercialization.

This achievement further strengthens 3D Systems’ relationships with the Defense Health Agency and the Department of Veterans Affairs and positions the company to support future initiatives in advanced, patient-specific medical manufacturing.

text:
Jun 27, 2026

Petition Update: 165 Signatures and Growing Thank you to everyone who has signed, shared, commented, messaged friends, and helped bring attention to this issue. We have reached 165 verified signatures, with 93 people signing this week, and we are now pushing toward the next goal of 200. This progress matters. This petition is not just a personal complaint or something I created on a whim. I am using the signatures, support, and personal stories from this petition to help show that there is a real access problem affecting military retirees and families in Puerto Rico. I am also sharing this information with Puerto Rico’s Resident Commissioner, Pablo José Hernández, and his office as this issue connects to H.R. 2632, the TRICARE Equality Act, which seeks to improve TRICARE administration in Puerto Rico. That is why your signature, share, and story matter. The veteran may receive care through the VA, but spouses, children, and dependents often rely on TRICARE. When TRICARE access does not work in Puerto Rico, the whole family feels it. Families may struggle to find providers, get appointments, understand claims, resolve billing issues, pay up front, or find offices that know how to properly process TRICARE. For some retirees, this becomes a painful decision: return home to Puerto Rico or stay in the mainland because healthcare access for their family is more reliable there. That should not be the choice. We served the same country. We followed the same orders. We paid into the same system. Our families sacrificed too. A healthcare benefit that works only on paper is not enough. Puerto Rico military retirees and families need access that works in real life. Please continue to sign and share.
